questions.question: So if I buy the levis 501 shrink to fit will they get tighter after washing?

hybrid.answer:
**Yes, they'll get tighter (smaller), but he says that's the point, and you plan for it by sizing up.**

**How much they shrink and how to size**
- In his most recent take (2025) he still likes the 501 Shrink-to-Fit: you put them in the bathtub and they shrink, so you should usually go two sizes up [1].
- He explains the denim is unsanforized, meaning untreated for shrinkage, and says it can shrink up to 10% on the first wash [2].
- His fuller sizing rule (2021): Levi's recommends two sizes bigger in the waist and two inches longer than you'd normally wear [3]. He says it took him four pairs of 501s to accept that Levi's is right. If you follow it, your jeans will "fit regularly" after they get wet [4].
- In his 2023 Wrangler comparison he went two sizes up (32s instead of his usual 30) [5]. After shrinking, the STFs ended up smaller than a regular rinsed pair of 501s [6].

**Washing affects how much they shrink**
He advises against tossing STFs in the dryer or rinsing them in very hot water. His pair looked "way better" because he did neither [7]. He notes that dryer-dried STFs would end up a lot smaller [8].

**They loosen up again with wear**
In his 2019 video he ignored the size-up advice. After a hot soak the waist was very tight, while the length barely changed [9]. A week later the waist and upper thigh had stretched enough that he could wear a belt [10]. In 2023 he also says he'd bet frequently worn STFs stretch back out [11].

**In short:** expect them to shrink, mostly in the waist. Size up two in the waist, go a bit longer, avoid very hot water and the dryer, and expect some give back as you wear them.

questions.question: Why do you cuff your jeans?

hybrid.answer:
For The Iron Snail, cuffing comes down to **length** and **leg shape**. His reasons have shifted a little over time:

**Most recent (July 2020, Levi's 501 one-year update):** He cuffs because he doesn't think his current style suits wider-legged pants worn uncuffed. His 501s were a 30 length and he says he would definitely have gotten a 32, but he'd have cuffed them anyway [1].

**Late 2019 (L.L. Bean boots review):** He said he always used to cuff his jeans but had started to prefer wearing them down over his boots [2]. He thinks letting jeans fall over boots calms down a loud piece like Bean boots, and he recommends a 7 or 7.5 inch leg opening pulled over the boot for a more workwear look [3].

**Mid-2019 (Levi's 501 STF video):** His main reason was length. To him, jeans that look too long just look bad, and he called that "the first and foremost thing." He also said the cuff shouldn't be too thick [4]. He used a pin roll to slim down wide legs: on his Gap 1969 jeans it made them taper more than normal [5]. On the very wide unshrunk 501s, a pin roll looked a little better but they were still too wide for him [6].

In short, he cuffs to get the length right and to keep wider jeans looking slimmer. With boots, though, he had started letting his jeans hang over them instead.

questions.question: How does the made in England boot stack up to Solovairs? [Dr. Martens]

hybrid.answer:
**Short version: in his April 2022 review, The Iron Snail favors Solovair over Made in England Dr. Martens for most people.** He calls Solovair cheaper and better built. The one reason he gives to pick the Made in England pair is if you want the yellow stitching.

**Where he thinks they're even**
- **Leather:** He says the Made in England boots' better leather will age fine and is "probably on par" with Solovair's [1].
- **Midsoles:** He also rates the Made in England midsoles as probably on par with Solovair's [2].

**Where he thinks Solovair wins**
- **Price:** He says Solovair boots are actually cheaper than Made in England Docs [3]. If you're going for pure value and want a better-built boot, Solovair is where he points you [4].
- **Shank and comfort:** Solovair boots have a shank, which he says makes them more comfortable over long periods [5]. Docs don't have one. The trade-off he notes is that Solovairs are tougher to break in but give you more comfort down the line [6].
- **Resoling:** He says Solovairs are Goodyear welted in a more commonly accepted way, so they're easier to resole [7].
- **Same boot, original maker:** He describes Solovair as one of the original makers of Doc Martens [5]. He says their derby eight-eye boot is "essentially the exact same boot" [8].

**Where Made in England wins**
- **Yellow stitching:** It's the only thing Solovair doesn't do [9]. If it matters to you, he says you have to get the Made in England Docs [10].

**Caveat about his Solovair pair**
After eight wears, a tab on the back of his right boot ripped off and a bootlace snapped [11]. He said he was sure it was a manufacturing defect and had contacted the company [12]. He also said he wasn't sponsored by either brand [13].

**Later update on Made in England (2023)**
In a May 2023 video he compared the Made in England 1460 with the cheaper Made in Thailand version, not with Solovair. He concluded the extra $90 is "probably not" worth it on a purely objective basis [14]. In his view they're mainly for mega fans of the brand [15]. He hasn't revisited the Solovair comparison since the 2022 video.

questions.question: Hi, I am going on a 4 day hike and I am wondering if I can use my blundstone for them, what do you think?

hybrid.answer:
The Iron Snail hasn't talked about multi-day hikes specifically, but he has hiked a fair bit in his own Blundstones. His view is that they **work for hiking, but they aren't ideal for serious mountain terrain**.

**What he found after a year (2020)**
- He wore them almost daily for about eight months and took them on a lot of hikes and up mountains [1].
- His main caveat is that they "are not good boots for mountaining apparently" because they lack good ankle support [2].
- He went up and down a few mountains in Maine. They got a little scuffed but "held up well" [3]. He says the scuffing was worse than he expected, partly because he kicks rocks on descents [4].
- On water, he thinks they're fine "if you're crossing a brook or a stream" or standing in mud for a bit. He wouldn't just stand in still water in them [5].

**His earlier take (2019)**
- He liked that they "can kind of go anywhere": winter boots, hiking or fashion [6].
- His recommendation came with a condition: "yes 100% if you're going to treat them." Otherwise he suggests plastic or Gore-Tex boots instead [7].
- If yours are a distressed style like rustic brown, he later pointed to Blundstone's own FAQ, which says those leathers "do not carry the same pretreatments" as finished, oiled leathers. You may want to condition them first [8].

**Applied to your trip:** going by what he's said, they should handle trails, mud and stream crossings. If your route has a lot of steep or rocky mountain sections, his ankle-support caveat is the main thing to weigh, and he'd want them well treated before you go. For dedicated hiking he also mentions owning Keens as his hiking boots [9].

**Short answer:** The Iron Snail has hiked a lot in his Blundstones and they held up, but he doesn't consider them proper mountain boots, mainly because of the lack of ankle support. He hasn't talked about multi-day hikes or carrying a heavy pack in them, so he hasn't directly answered whether they'd suit a 4-day trip.

**What he's said about hiking in them**
- In his one-year review (2020), he says he wore them on a lot of hikes and climbed a lot of mountains in them [1]. He also notes that they are not good boots for mountains because they don't have good ankle support [2].
- He went up and down a few mountains in Maine; they got a little scuffed up but held up well [3].
- His wider verdict is that they're decent for work but not incredible. He sees them as a balanced, everyday walking boot and says you should get the right tool for the job [4].
- His girlfriend also wore hers on hikes and snowshoeing without treating them, and they still looked great [5].

**Break-in**
Even after a lot of wear, he got big break-in blisters once he started walking long distances and running in them. These only stopped after two to three weeks [6]. If your pair isn't well broken in yet, that's worth thinking about before a long trip.

**Water**
In his pond test, he concluded you should be fine crossing a brook or stream or standing in mud for a little while [7]. Years later, he still called them probably his most water-resistant boots [8].

**Care**
His original recommendation came with a condition: buy them only if you're going to keep them treated [9]. His rule of thumb is that if the leather looks or feels dry, or water isn't beading on top, it probably needs more wax [10]. Applied to your trip, it would make sense to clean and treat them beforehand.

So, going by his experience, they can handle hiking, streams and mud. The thing he flagged for rough mountain terrain is ankle support, and he hasn't said anything about multi-day loads.

questions.question: 1907 vs the 875's? What's the difference?

hybrid.answer:
**Short version:** The Iron Snail sees the 1907 as the better buy of the two. Both are Red Wing moc toes, but for about $10 more the 1907 adds a storm welt, a removable leather footbed and leather laces [1][2].

**The main differences he points out (2021):**
- **Welt construction.** The 875 is Goodyear welted, which he calls incredible: really durable and pretty water resistant, with room for a cork filling that molds to your foot [3]. The 1907 has what Red Wing calls a storm welt, sometimes described as "Norwegian-like" [4]. He reports the popular view he's seen on Reddit that Red Wing's version is basically an extra strip of leather stitched onto the welt, but he says he's not quite sure [5]. To him, the storm welt is "invaluable" [2].
- **Extras for the price.** The 1907 comes with Red Wing's leather footbed, which he says usually costs $40 on its own. He likes that you can pull it out at night so the boots dry faster. It also comes with leather laces he values at about $15. He first says that's $55 of freebies, then corrects it to technically $45 once you subtract the extra $10 [2].
- **His verdict then:** if you're looking at a Red Wing moc toe, he thinks you should get the 1907s [6].

**How the 1907 did in his water test:** one boot leaked almost immediately through the stitching, which he calls a letdown, while the other stayed dry. Even so, he has no doubt they'd hold up fine in rain, grass or mud [7].

**What they share:** both use crepe soles. He says he doesn't really like those [8] and worries they'll break down faster than a dense Vibram sole [9]. He also calls both 1907s and 875s "more beefily constructed" heritage boots, good if you need a tough boot [10].

**His later take:** in 2022 he said his Red Wing 3335s beat both the 1907s and the 875s as an all-around boot for hikes and walks in the woods [10]. By 2023 he was less sure the 3335s were still his favourite, saying the 875s, 1907s and Iron Rangers "all have their own characteristics" that he really likes [11]. He hasn't revisited the 1907-vs-875 matchup directly since 2021.

questions.question: How does Uniqlo compare to The Front General Store,  Proclub, and Hanes? ie what is the best budget shirt?

hybrid.answer:
**Short version:** In his most recent videos, The Iron Snail treats **Uniqlo as the best budget t-shirt for the money**. **The Front General Store** is his pick for a step up at around $40. He liked **Pro Club** and **Hanes** when he tried them in 2024, but he has never put them head-to-head with Uniqlo. Later he lumped Hanes in with the ultra-cheap mass-market brands, where his shirts had defects.

**Uniqlo: his budget benchmark**
- In his September 2025 roundup he says the $20 Uniqlo tee "is probably the best t-shirt that you can get bar none for the price" [1]. He calls it "your starter t-shirt", though the fabric is open-end and "kind of rough" [2].
- If you're taller or wider, he suggests Muji instead. It costs a few dollars more but is significantly longer and wider [2].
- In June 2025 he praised its bound neck collar and called the price-to-quality ratio "insane" [3]. He wears the black one all the time [3].
- Back in 2024 he gave the Uniqlo heavyweight crew neck his "best value heavyweight or all-around" award and the Uniqlo Supima tee "best value silky smooth" [4].

**The Front General Store: the upgrade pick**
- In 2024 he said that if you want a Japanese-made shirt, or just an upgrade, without spending over $40, it's "one of the best shirts that you could possibly get" [5].
- He thinks it uses open-end yarn that has been sanded for softness. He scored it 6/10 for softness, and it barely shrank because it's pre-washed [5].
- He still calls it "still really good" in 2025 [6]. In his latest roundup he describes it as a $40, 100% made-in-Japan shirt with "great proportions, great feel" [2].

**Pro Club**
- He hadn't heard of it until fans suggested it. After trying it he said "I really like proc Club" [7].
- He calls it an old-school American shirt and the roughest on his list (softness 4/10). It has a high neck hole with Lycra that supposedly keeps its shape [7].
- It shrank quite a bit in length, about 6.86% [7].

**Hanes**
- In 2024 he called it "your classic $10 great shirt" [8]. He found it much softer and lighter than Pro Club, with a similar fit but slightly lower armholes [7].
- He scored it 7/10 for softness, but it shrank about 6.73% in length [8].
- By June 2025 he was grouping Hanes and Gildan together as rock-bottom, mass-market brands. All five shirts he had from those brands had a defect of some kind [9].

**So which is best?**
- For the lowest price with dependable quality, he leans **Uniqlo**.
- For about double the money, **Front General Store** is his upgrade.
- He also flags a few other values:
  - In mid-2025 he rated Bronson and Bravestar Selvage "slightly above Uniclo" on value at around $29–32 [10].
  - House of Blanks at $35 is "truly an outstanding value" [11].
  - If you just want the cheapest decent shirt, he called the Kirkland six-pack (about $4.20 a shirt) fantastic [12].
